'''Richard Jed Wyatt''' (June 5, 1939<ref name="nyt" /> – 7 June 2002) was an American psychiatrist and [[schizophrenia]] researcher.<ref name="nih">{{Cite web | url=https://wwwapp.nimh.nih.gov/str/static/RichardWyatt713.pdf | title=Richard Jed Wyatt (1937-2002)}}</ref>

==Career and Research==
Wyatt was born in [[Los Angeles]] and graduated from [[Johns Hopkins University Medical School]]<ref name="nih"/> and joined the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) in 1967, where he established a schizophrenia research program. In 1972 he became chief of the [[neuropsychiatry]] branch at the NIH.<ref name="nyt"/> He was one of the early pioneers who studied the biological basis of schizophrenia in the lab.<ref name="nih"/> His research led to the first evidence that [[Monoamine oxidase inhibitor|monoamine oxidase inhibitors]] (MAOIs) suppressed [[REM sleep]] and could treat [[narcolepsy]].<ref name="nih"/>

He was a writer, educator and teacher, having authored over 800 research articles and 6 books and He has trained many [[Neuroscientist|neuroscientists]].<ref name="nyt"/><ref name="nih"/> The [[Richard J. Wyatt Award]] from the [[International Early Intervention and Prevention in Mental Health Association]] is named after him in recognition of his work on early interventions in schizophrenia.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Awards |url=https://iepa.org.au/Awards |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=IEPA}}</ref>

He was married to Rollyn Simon Wyatt and later to [[clinical psychologist]] and author [[Kay Redfield Jamison]].<ref name="nyt" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Zielinkski |first=Graeme |date=2002-06-12 |title=Schizophrenia Expert Richard J. Wyatt Dies |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2002/06/12/schizophrenia-expert-richard-j-wyatt-dies/b2664bfa-cf65-47c9-a0da-6e94e444ed2a/ |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> He had three children.<ref name="nyt"/><ref name=":1" /> With Jamison he co-produced several films about [[Manic-depressive illness|manic depressive illness]].<ref name="nih"/> Wyatt died of [[lung cancer]] on 7 June 2002 at the age of 63 in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name="nyt">{{Cite news |last1=O'Connor |first1=Anahad |author-link=Anahad O'Connor |date=2002-06-12 |title=Richard J. Wyatt, 63, is Dead; Led Studies of Schizophrenia |pages=A27 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/06/12/us/richard-j-wyatt-63-is-dead-led-studies-of-schizophrenia.html |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Weinberger |first=Daniel R. |author-link=Daniel R. Weinberger |date=October 2002 |title=Richard Jed Wyatt, 1939–2002 |journal=[[Neuropsychopharmacology (journal)|Neuropsychopharmacology]] |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=687–689 |doi=10.1016/S0893-133X(02)00414-1|s2cid=11537467 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Jamison authored a 2009 book, ''Nothing Was the Same: A Memoir'', recounting her relationship with Wyatt and the process of grieving after his death.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lindbergh |first=Reeve |author-link=Reeve Lindbergh |date=2009-10-16 |title='Nothing Was the Same': Kay Redfield Jamison's memoir of love and grief |work=[[The Seattle Times]] |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/entertainment/books/nothing-was-the-same-kay-redfield-jamisons-memoir-of-love-and-grief/ |issn=0745-9696}}</ref>
